title: Taiwan detains an Nvidia employee as its chip-smuggling probe reaches the chipmaker
excerpt: Taiwan’s investigation into smuggled AI hardware, which began with Super Micro and had spent months working through the island’s distributors, has now reached inside Nvidia itself. content_html:
Taiwan’s investigation into smuggled AI hardware, which began with Super Micro and had spent months working through the island’s distributors, has now reached inside Nvidia itself.

On July 28, prosecutors detained an Nvidia employee as part of the probe into whether restricted AI servers were being routed to China, Bloomberg first reported, the first time the widening case has touched the company whose processors sit at the centre of it.

The employee, whom local media identified as a senior business-development manager, was held by the Keelung District Prosecutors’ Office, which has driven the case since spring.

Prosecutors allege he signed off on end-user and “know your customer” documents that helped restricted Nvidia servers clear export review before the hardware was diverted to China, according to Taiwanese press accounts of the case.

He has not been charged, and the allegations have not been tested in court. Much of this began as the first criminal probe of its kind on the island.

The investigation grew out of something unrelated. Coast Guard officers working a drug-smuggling case stumbled onto an underground supply chain, and the chip thread has since pulled in Super Micro and several of its Taiwanese distribution and data-centre partners.

Investigators say roughly 50 servers built around Nvidia’s GB300 Grace Blackwell Ultra chips, together worth about NT$700 million, or some $21 million, were seized in May.

Prosecutors allege shell companies placed the orders and the machines were then parked in a Taiwanese data centre to look as though they had never left the island, before being routed onward through third countries. Earlier reporting pointed to Japan as one such transshipment point on the way to Hong Kong and mainland China.

Because Taiwan has no law that directly criminalises exporting AI chips to China, prosecutors have leaned on charges of document forgery and breach of trust.

“It’s not a criminal violation in Taiwan to export AI chips to China, obviously it is under US law,” Chris McGuire, a fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, told Bloomberg.

A proposed amendment to Taiwan’s Foreign Trade Act would close that gap, though it has not yet passed, which leaves prosecutors building a smuggling case on paperwork offences rather than on the exports themselves.

The detention widens a case that had, until now, centred on Super Micro. Prosecutors moved to detain three people in May, including Super Micro co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw, and held further Super Micro staff through July.

The company has said it is cooperating, that it is not itself a target of the investigation, and that it suspended four Taiwan-based employees connected to the matter.

The Taiwanese proceedings run in parallel with a US case. In March, the Justice Department unsealed an indictment alleging a $2.5 billion scheme to divert Nvidia-powered servers to China through falsified documents and decoy shipments, with Liaw among those charged.

That case turned on falsified end-user paperwork, unmarked boxes, and a pass-through firm, a set of tactics that echoes the document offences Taiwanese prosecutors are now pursuing.

Washington has restricted sales of Nvidia’s most advanced processors to China since 2022, and enforcement has struggled to keep pace with demand, a gap the dummy-server indictment laid bare.

Nvidia has consistently said it complies with export controls and cannot service or support products that reach customers through illicit channels. Jensen Huang has called black-market data centres assembled from smuggled parts a dead end, arguing that diverted chips are effectively useless without the company’s continued technical support.

The company had not commented publicly on the detention of its own employee at the time of writing.

What happens next runs through the Keelung court, which will decide whether the Nvidia employee is held further or released on bail while the inquiry continues. For a case that started with a drug bust and a shipping container, it has travelled a long way up the supply chain.

content_html_zh:
台湾对走私人工智能硬件的调查始于超微公司，花了数月时间通过台湾的分销商进行调查，现在已经深入到英伟达内部。

彭博社首先报道称，7 月 28 日，检察官拘留了一名 Nvidia 员工，以调查受限制的人工智能服务器是否被路由到中国，这是这一不断扩大的案件首次触及该公司的处理器。

当地媒体确认这名员工是一名高级业务开发经理，目前已被基隆地方检察厅拘留，自春季以来，基隆地方检察厅一直在推动此案。

据台湾媒体对此案的报道，检察官指控他签署了最终用户和“了解你的客户”文件，这些文件帮助受限制的英伟达服务器在硬件被转移到中国之前通过了出口审查。

他没有受到指控，这些指控也没有在法庭上得到检验。 其中大部分是岛上首次此类刑事调查。

这项调查源于一些不相关的事情。 处理毒品走私案件的海岸警卫队官员偶然发现了一条地下供应链，此后芯片线索吸引了超微及其几家台湾分销和数据中心合作伙伴。

调查人员表示，5 月份查获了大约 50 台基于 Nvidia GB300 Grace Blackwell Ultra 芯片的服务器，总价值约新台币 7 亿元（约合 2100 万美元）。

检察官指控空壳公司下了订单，然后将这些机器停放在台湾的一个数据中心，看起来好像它们从未离开过台湾，然后再通过第三国继续运送。 早些时候的报道指出，日本是前往香港和中国大陆的转运点之一。

由于台湾没有直接将向中国出口人工智能芯片定为刑事犯罪的法律，检察官倾向于以伪造文件和违反信任的罪名进行指控。

美国外交关系委员会研究员克里斯·麦奎尔对彭博社表示：“台湾向中国出口人工智能芯片并不构成刑事犯罪，显然这是根据美国法律的。”

台湾《对外贸易法》的拟议修正案将缩小这一差距，尽管该修正案尚未通过，这使得检察官根据文书犯罪而不是出口本身来立案走私。

此次拘留扩大了迄今为止以超微为中心的案件范围。 检察官于 5 月采取行动拘留了三人，其中包括 Super Micro 联合​​创始人 Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw，并在 7 月期间拘留了更多 Super Micro 员工。

该公司表示正在配合，其本身并非调查目标，并已停职四名与此事有关的台湾员工。

台湾的诉讼程序与美国的案件同时进行。 今年 3 月，司法部公布了一份起诉书，指控一项价值 25 亿美元的计划，通过伪造文件和诱饵货物将 Nvidia 驱动的服务器转移到中国，Liaw 也在其中。

该案涉及伪造的最终用户文件、未标记的盒子和一家转手公司，这一系列策略与台湾检察官目前正在追查的文件犯罪相呼应。

自 2022 年以来，华盛顿一直限制英伟达最先进的处理器向中国销售，而且执法力度一直难以满足需求，虚拟服务器起诉书暴露了这一差距。

英伟达一直表示，它遵守出口管制，不能为通过非法渠道到达客户的产品提供服务或支持。 黄仁勋称用走私零件组装的黑市数据中心是一条死胡同，他认为如果没有公司持续的技术支持，转移的芯片实际上毫无用处。

截至撰写本文时，该公司尚未就其员工被拘留一事公开发表评论。

接下来发生的事情将由基隆法院审理，该法院将在调查继续期间决定是否进一步拘留或保释这名 Nvidia 员工。 对于一个以缉获毒品和一个集装箱开始的案件来说，它已经在供应链上走了很长一段路。
